q: You are halfway across on the ARC, converting the almanac's LMT to UT by hand. What is your longitude in time?
Your ship's clocks keep the Caribbean zone time. What do you write in the UT column of the log?
why: West longitude, ZD +4: UT = zone time + ZD = 1530 + 4 h = 1930.

q: You take a sun sight on the passage from Bermuda to the Azores. What UT goes into the reduction?
why: A fast watch shows too much: UT = 14 23 10 − 12 s = 14 22 58.

fig.title: Deck watch
lines: Error on GPS this morning: 12 s fast

q: Checking the watch after landfall, you find it was 8 seconds out during the last day's sights. How much longitude error did that put in your sun lines?
why: The Earth turns 15′ of arc per minute of time: 4 s = 1′ of longitude, so 8 s = 2′.

fig.title: After landfall
lines: Not applied to the last day's sights

q: Bound west from Tonga to Fiji, you cross the 180th meridian at 2100 on Tuesday 9 June, ship's time. What do you write in the log a moment later?
why: Westbound across 180° the date goes forward a day (ZD +12 becomes −12); the clock time stays the same.

q: Your logs hold noon sights from passages all through the year, and the almanac's Mer Pass for the Sun moves. Why?
a: The true Sun runs ahead of or behind the mean Sun
o: The ship's clocks are changed for summer time
The Earth's spin speeds up and slows down
why: Mean time runs evenly, the true Sun does not (elliptic orbit, tilted axis): the difference is the equation of time, up to ~16 min.

q: Your crew asks whether the radio's UTC must be corrected before you open the almanac. What do you tell them?
a: Use it as UT; the difference is under a second
o: Add 18 s to it to get UT
Add 37 s to it to get UT
Apply the zone description to it first
why: UTC is kept within 0.9 s of UT; 0.9 s is about 0.2′ of longitude, below what a sextant can give.

q: Your crew keeps the deck log in ship's time, which changes as you go west. Which time do you write against every sight and fix?
a: UT, read from the deck watch
o: Ship's time, as the crew does
The zone time of the port you left
why: Sights and fixes are worked in UT; ship's time jumps an hour at every zone change, UT never does.

fig.title: Nav log, day 9
lines: Ship's clocks retarded 1 h last night
Crew log events in ship's time

q: You are alone on deck at dawn with the sextant, and the deck watch is below at the chart table. How do you time the star sight?
a: Start a stopwatch at the sight; compare it with the watch later
o: Read the watch when you get back to the chart table
Note the minute only; the seconds hardly matter
Take the time of the plotter's last GPS fix
why: Start the stopwatch at the instant of the sight, then subtract its reading from the watch time; never guess the seconds.

q: You work a sun sight by hand. How do you get the GHA for the moment of the sight?
a: The 14h GHA plus the increment for 23m 10s
o: The 14h GHA alone; minutes are below sextant accuracy
The 14h GHA plus 0°23′10″ for the minutes
The 14h GHA plus the v correction for 23m
why: The daily page gives GHA for each whole hour; the increments page adds the minutes and seconds (15° an hour for the Sun).

q: South of Hispaniola with the GPS down, you time the moment the Sun stops rising at noon. What longitude does that give you?
why: 16 37 20 − 12 00 00 = 4h 37m 20s: 60° + 9°15′ + 5′ = 69°20′, west because local noon comes after Greenwich's.

q: You plan the evening star sights off the Queensland coast. At what UT does the Sun set?
why: 147°45′ = 9h 51m; east longitude: UT = LMT − 9h 51m = 1735 − 0951 = 0744 UT, the same date.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: You keep ship's time by the zone you are in. Which zone description belongs to this noon position?
why: Zone +3 runs from 37°30′W to 52°30′W, centred on 45°W; 37°40′W is just inside it.

q: You want to compare the deck watch with a radio time signal. What UT and date is it now?
why: East longitude, ZD −10: UT = 0930 − 10 h = 2330 on the day before, 13 May.

q: You sail the ARC from Las Palmas to Rodney Bay and keep ship's time by the zone you are in. How do the clocks change on the way?
a: Retard 3 h, an hour each at 22°30′W, 37°30′W and 52°30′W
o: Advance 3 h, an hour each at 22°30′W, 37°30′W and 52°30′W
Retard 4 h, an hour each at 15°W, 30°W, 45°W and 60°W
Retard 3 h, an hour each at 30°W, 45°W and 60°W
why: Westbound the zones go from +1 to +4: retard an hour at each boundary, 7°30′ past each multiple of 15°.

q: You keep zone time on the passage east. What do you do with the ship's clocks now?
why: Eastbound you enter zone +3 at 52°30′W: advance the clocks an hour; the ZD falls by one.

q: You clear in at Horta, and the office closes at 1730 local time. What time is it ashore as you tie up?
why: UT = 1500 + 2 h = 1700; the Azores keep UT +0 in summer, so it is 1700 ashore.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

q: After the Puddle Jump you anchor in Taiohae Bay. What is the local time ashore?
why: UT = 1400 + 9 h = 2300; the Marquesas keep UT −9 h 30 m: 2300 − 0930 = 1330 local.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

q: You are on passage to Fiji and join the cruisers' SSB net. When do you switch the radio on, by ship's time?
why: ZD −12: ship's time = UT + 12 h = 0300 + 12 h = 1500 on the same Thursday.

q: On 16 November you still have no time signal. What are the watch's daily rate and its error now?
a: Gaining 2 s a day; 31 s fast
o: Gaining 14 s a day; 115 s fast
Losing 2 s a day; 3 s fast
Gaining 2.4 s a day; 34 s fast
why: (17 − 3) s / 7 days = gaining 2 s a day; 17 s + 7 × 2 s = 31 s fast on 16 Nov.

q: You check the deck watch against the GPS just before a morning sun sight. What UT do you use for the sight?
why: The watch is 7 s ahead of the GPS, so 7 s fast: 09 41 18 − 7 s = 09 41 11 UT.

q: Mid-Atlantic, your watch is 20 seconds fast and you do not know it. Where does that put your positions from sun lines?
why: Too late a UT gives too big a GHA; west longitude = GHA − LHA comes out 20 s × 15″ = 5′ too far west.

fig.title: Celestial-only passage
lines: Sun lines worked with that time

q: Your crew set the deck watch from the plotter, which shows GPS time. What error does that put in your longitude?
why: GPS time runs 18 s ahead of UTC (no leap seconds); 18 s × 15″ = 270″ = 4.5′ of longitude.

q: You need a reliable time check for your sights. Where do you get it?
a: Time signals on the SSB, e.g. WWV on 10 MHz
o: The bulkhead clock, set before departure
The laptop clock, synced in port
The VHF's log of the last DSC call
why: Shortwave time stations (WWV/WWVH on 5, 10, 15 MHz) give UTC to the second; clocks set weeks ago have unknown errors.

fig.title: Day 12, no GPS
lines: Plotter and both GPS sets dead

q: Alone on deck, you time a sun sight this way. What is the UT of the sight?
why: 10 15 00 − 1m 37s = 10 13 23 by the watch; it is 4 s fast, so UT 10 13 19.

q: Your crew misread the minute when calling the time of a sun sight. How big an error does that put in your longitude?
why: The Sun's GHA moves 15° an hour, 15′ a minute: one minute of time wrong moves the line 15′ of longitude.

q: Bound east from New Zealand to Tahiti, you cross the 180th meridian on Friday 15 May, ship's time. What date goes in the log after the next midnight?
why: Eastbound across 180° you repeat a day (ZD −12 becomes +12): Friday 15 May comes twice.

q: Bound west from Suwarrow to Samoa, you take a star sight at dusk. Which almanac page and hour do you open?
why: ZD +11: UT = 1850 + 11 h = 0550 the next day: the 5 May page, the 05h row.

q: Approaching Suva, you take a morning sun sight. With which date and time do you enter the almanac?
why: ZD −12: UT = 0745 − 12 h = 1945 on 14 March; the almanac is entered with the UT date, not the ship's.

q: Between Tahiti and the Cook Islands you download a GRIB file. At what ship's time is this forecast valid?
why: ZD +10: ship's time = UT − 10 h = 1200 − 10 h = 0200 on the same date.

q: On the ARC you work a sun sight by hand. What is the Sun's GHA at the moment of the sight?
In the Indian Ocean at dawn you take a star sight. What is GHA Aries at the moment of the sight?
In the trade winds on the day of the equinox you work a sun sight. Which declination do you use?
why: d 1.0′ an hour × 48/60 = 0.8′ northward: S 0°00.6′ − 0.8′ crosses the equator, Dec N 0°00.2′.

q: West of the Cape Verdes you plan the noon sight. At what UT does the Sun cross your meridian?
why: Mer Pass is LMT: 23°15′W = 1h 33m; west, so UT = 1144 + 0133 = 1317 UT.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: Leaving Cape Town for St Helena, you want a noon sight. What is the UT of local noon?
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: A crew member says you must also apply the equation of time to the Mer Pass to get local noon. When is local noon, in LMT?
why: The Mer Pass is already 1200 + 14m 13s with the EoT applied; only your longitude is left, to turn it into UT.

q: On the ARC you want the watch called for sunrise. At what ship's time does the Sun rise?
why: UT = 0625 + 2h 44m = 0909; ship's time = 0909 − 3 h = 0609, 16 min before LMT since you are east of 45°W.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: You want to be on deck with the sextant when morning nautical twilight begins. What ship's time is that?
why: UT = 0536 − 3h 50m = 0146; ship's time = 0146 + 4 h = 0546, 10 min after LMT since you are west of 60°E.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: Bound from Rio towards Tristan da Cunha, you plan the dusk star sights. At what UT does the Sun set?
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: You arrive at the marina in Mindelo. What time is it ashore?
why: UT = 1000 + 2 h = 1200; the islands keep UT −1, so 1100 ashore: legal time need not match the nautical zone.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

fig.title: Mindelo, Cape Verde
lines: Cape Verde keeps UT −1 all year

q: Between the Cook Islands and Niue you plan the dusk star sights. What are the UT and the date of sunset?
why: 165° = 11h 00m; west, so UT = 1823 + 11 h = 0523 UT on the next day, 4 March.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: The GPS has been dead since 1 December. What UT do you use for this sight?
why: 6 s slow, then 20 days × 1.5 s gained = 30 s: now 24 s fast; UT = 10 14 32 − 24 s = 10 14 08.

q: Approaching the Bay of Biscay you find the watch was 30 seconds slow for the whole crossing. How far, and which way, is your fix wrong?
why: 30 s = 7.5′ of longitude; a slow watch puts you east; 7.5′ × cos 48° = 5.0 M on the ground.

fig.title: Bound for Brittany, lat 48°N
lines: Fix from sun and star lines

q: You plan your arrival in Tonga and book the customs officer. What will the local time and date be when you arrive?
why: UT out 1800 on 1 June + 7 d 2 h = 2000 UT on 8 June; Tonga keeps UT +13: 0900 on 9 June.

q: You take the first star of the morning round. Which almanac entries do you use?
why: 23 59 58 + 3 s = 00 00 01 UT on 7 Nov: the 00h row of 7 Nov plus the increment for 1 second.

fig.title: Dawn stars, Indian Ocean
lines: Deck watch keeps UT, 3 s slow

q: On your way into the South Atlantic you plan the dusk star sights. At what ship's time does the Sun set?
why: 5°N is halfway: 1742 LMT; UT = 1742 + 2h 20m = 2002; ship's time = 2002 − 2 h = 1802.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: You want to time the noon sight exactly, to get a longitude from it. At what UT does the Sun cross your meridian?

fig.title: Noon to the second, 4 November
lines: EoT 16m 29s, Sun ahead of mean time

q: At the end of the ARC you work a sun sight timed by the cockpit watch. What is the Sun's GHA?

fig.title: Almanac, 10 December
lines: Watch on ship's time (ZD +3), 5 s slow

q: You want to close the coast after sunrise. What will the ship's clock show when the Sun rises?
why: UT = 0612 + 4h 04m = 1016; on ZD +3 the clock shows 1016 − 3 h = 0716 (0616 only after you go to ZD +4).
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: You plan the evening star sights for the window between civil and nautical twilight. What is that window by ship's time?
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: Closing Western Australia from Mauritius, you turn the almanac's LMT of sunrise into UT. How much time does your longitude give, and which way do you apply it?
why: 115° × 4 min = 460 min, 45′ = 3 min: 7h 43m. East of Greenwich LMT is ahead of UT, so UT = LMT − 7h 43m.

fig.title: DR, approaching Fremantle
lines: Almanac sunrise is given in LMT

q: On passage to the Maldives you log a fix taken at this time. What UT goes beside it?
why: East longitude, ZD −5: UT = zone time + ZD = 1400 − 5 h = 0900. The ZD, not the exact longitude, sets ship's time.

q: Running south well off the Brazilian coast, you take an afternoon sun sight. What UT goes into the reduction?
why: A slow watch shows too little: add the error. UT = 16 05 54 + 9 s = 16 06 03.

fig.title: Deck watch
lines: Compared with GPS at noon: 9 s slow

q: Bound west from Niue for Fiji, you cross the 180th meridian tonight and change the ship's date. What do you do with the deck watch you keep on UT?
a: Nothing — UT and its date run on unchanged
o: Put its date forward a day with the ship's
Put its date back a day for the crossing
Reset it to the new zone time, ZD −12
why: The date line changes zone time and the ship's date only; UT is the same on both sides, so the deck watch and its date are left alone.

q: You check the deck watch against the hourly time signal on the radio. At which moment is it exactly the hour?
a: At the start of the sixth, long pip
o: At the start of the first pip
At the end of the sixth, long pip
At the end of the fifth, short pip
why: The pips count down the last five seconds; the hour is the start of the last, longer pip.

fig.title: Broadcast time signal
lines: Five short pips, then one long one

q: Last night you watched the Moon cross your meridian. About when will it cross tonight?
why: The Moon moves east round the sky about 13° a day, so it reaches your meridian some 50 min later each day (40–66 min).

q: Your rate book shows the deck watch gaining faster since you reached the tropics. What is the likely cause, and what do you do?
a: Heat; use the new rate from recent checks
o: Zone changes; add 1 s per hour retarded
A failing battery; average the two rates
Magnetism; move it from the chart table
why: A quartz watch's rate changes with temperature: predict its error with the rate measured in the present climate.

fig.title: Rate book
lines: Falmouth to Madeira: gaining 0.4 s a day
Since the Cape Verdes: gaining 1.6 s a day
Watch kept in the chart table

q: You work a dawn sight of Canopus by hand. Which increment do you add to the 03h GHA of Aries?
why: Stars go through GHA Aries, which turns 15°02.46′ an hour, so it has its own column; the seconds count too (4 s = 1′).

q: Westbound on the trade-wind crossing, you retard the clocks tonight. How long is watch B on deck?
why: At 0200 the clock goes back to 0100: B stands 0000 to 0400 by the clock, which is 5 hours of real time.
ref: Time — ship's time and the watch rota

q: Your old handheld GPS from the grab bag shows this. What do you take from its display?
a: Its time of day; the date comes from the log
o: Nothing; its clock is corrupt as well
Its date and time; a GPS is never wrong
Its time less 19 years of leap seconds
why: An old receiver's week counter rolls over after 1024 weeks: the date jumps back 19.6 years, but the time of day stays right.

fig.title: Spare handheld GPS
lines: Time agrees with the radio signal

q: Between Cocos Keeling and Christmas Island with the GPS down, you time the Sun at its highest. What longitude does that give?
why: Local noon = 12 00 00 + 14m 08s = 12 14 08 LMT; less 05 31 44 UT = 6h 42m 24s east = 100°36′E.

fig.title: Noon, 15 February
lines: Watch checked on the radio today

q: Crossing the Indian Ocean from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues, you plan the ship's clock changes for the crew. What are they?
why: Westbound the zones go from −6 to −4: retard an hour at each boundary, 82°30′E and 67°30′E (7°30′ past 75° and 60°).

q: On the last clock change watch B stood five hours, and three more changes come before St Lucia. How do you plan them?
a: Retard 20 minutes in each of the three night watches
o: Retard the full hour at 0200 each time, as before
Advance the clocks instead, and catch up at landfall
Give B the extra hour each time, then a lie-in
why: Retarding 20 min in each night watch shares the hour: each watch stands 4h 20m, and no one stands five hours.
ref: Time — ship's time and the watch rota

fig.title: ARC rota, westbound

Last change at 0200: B stood 5 h

q: On passage from Richards Bay to Mauritius the boat crosses a zone boundary on this watch. What happens to the ship's clocks?
why: Eastbound the clocks go forward an hour at each boundary; in east longitude the ZD grows more negative: −2 becomes −3.

q: Off New Caledonia on New Year's morning you take a sun sight. Which almanac and which page do you open?
why: ZD −11: UT = 0730 − 11 h = 2030 on 31 December 2026 — the last page of last year's almanac.

q: Approaching Port Vila, you note the time of sunrise in the log in UT. What UT and date do you write?
why: 168°E = 11h 12m; UT = 0535 − 11h 12m = 1823 on the day before, 9 October. East of Greenwich, UT is behind.
ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

q: Off the Brazilian coast at 20°S you plan the evening star sights. Which planets can you add to them?
why: Venus and Mars cross with the Sun and are lost in its glare; at dusk Saturn is high in the west and Jupiter low in the east.
ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

q: Bound for Reykjavik in June, you look up tonight's star sights in the almanac. What does it tell you?
a: The sky never gets dark: plan on sun lines, not stars
o: Twilight lasts all night: shoot stars at any hour
The data is missing: interpolate from 60°N
The Sun stays up: take sun lines all night too
why: //// means the Sun never gets 6° below the horizon at 64°N: no dark sky with a horizon for stars; the Sun is up 21 hours.

q: You arrive at Puerto Williams in the Beagle Channel for Christmas. At what time by the clocks ashore does the Sun set?
why: UT = 2039 + 4h 30m = 0109 the next day; ashore UT − 3 h = 2209: far south at midsummer, on a zone east of its longitude.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

fig.title: Puerto Williams, 20 December
lines: Ship's clock ZD +5; Chile keeps UT −3

q: In the Bay of Bengal you want the Moon on your meridian for a latitude. At what UT does it cross tonight?
why: East: use the difference from the day before, 45 min × 90/360 = 11 min earlier: 2014 LMT; UT = 2014 − 6 h = 1414.

q: Under the midnight sun off Svalbard you want to time the Sun at its lowest, due north. At what UT does that come?
why: Lower transit at 0000 LMT + 2m 35s = 0003 LMT on 25 June; 15°E is 1 h, so UT = 2303 on 24 June.

fig.title: Off Svalbard, night of 24–25 June
lines: The Sun stays about 9° up all night

q: Off Mauritius before dawn you want Jupiter on your meridian for a latitude. At what ship's time does it cross?
why: A planet's Mer Pass is LMT, much the same at any longitude: UT = 0421 − 3h 52m = 0029; ship's time = UT + 4 h = 0429.
ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

q: In the Indian Ocean in February you plan to catch Sirius as it crosses your meridian. When is that by the ship's clock?
ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

q: The GPS failed a week ago. Before the morning sights you compare your three watches. Which one do you set aside, and what is UT?
why: Corrected, A and B both give 10 00 00 and C gives 10 00 30: C has jumped, and the two that agree give UT.

o: A has jumped 30 s; it has the bigger rate
Each is 15 s out; split the difference
Both are right; the heat changed the rates
why: Two watches show only their difference: one has jumped 30 s, but which one takes a third clock or a radio time signal.

q: Six days after the last GPS check, deep in the trades, you need the deck watch error for a sight. What is it now?

q: In the Indian Ocean at 70°E your watch is 12 seconds fast and you do not know it. What does that do to the longitude of your fixes?
a: 3′ too small — the fix lies too far west
o: 3′ too large — the fix lies too far east
12′ too small — the fix lies too far west
12′ too large — the fix lies too far east
why: Too late a time makes GHA too big; LHA = GHA + long E, so the east longitude comes out 3′ (12 s ÷ 4) too small: too far west.

q: In the Southern Ocean at 60°S you want each sun line good to a mile east–west. How large a watch error can you accept?
why: At 60° a mile of easting is 1′ ÷ cos 60° = 2′ of longitude, and 2′ of longitude is 8 s of time.

q: Checking the watch on a radio signal, you find it was two minutes wrong all yesterday. Which of yesterday's results can you still trust?
o: The running fix from all three
why: A meridian altitude needs no exact time, only the Dec, which barely moves in 2 min; the sun lines are 30′ of longitude out.

q: At dawn you shoot three stars alone, timing them with the stopwatch's lap button. What UT do you write for the second star?
why: The watch read 06 12 00 at UT 06 12 03; the second lap adds 4m 51s: UT 06 16 54.

q: You take a star at the very end of the hour. What is GHA Aries for the sight?
why: 02h row plus the Aries increment for 59m 59s, 15°02.2′: 83°11.6′ + 15°02.2′ = 98°13.8′, a hair short of the 03h value.

q: Heading for the Cape Verdes in February you work a sun sight. Which declination do you use?
why: The d correction for 37m at d 0.7 is 0.4′; the Dec is falling, so subtract: S 16°42.9′ − 0.4′ = S 16°42.5′.

q: Arriving in the Galápagos from Panama, you want to enter Academy Bay after sunrise. When does the Sun rise ashore, and by your ship's clock?
why: UT = 0610 + 6h 01m = 1211; ashore UT − 6 h = 0611; your clock, still on Panama's UT − 5, shows 0711.

fig.title: Santa Cruz, Galápagos, 15 Feb

q: After the passage from Tonga you berth at the Opua quarantine dock in November. Customs want you before 1700 New Zealand time. What is the time ashore now?
why: UT = 1500 − 12 h = 0300; New Zealand summer time is UT + 13: 1600 ashore, an hour ahead of your zone time.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

q: Looking at the almanac's Sun column in July, a crew member asks why the GHA at 12h is not 0°. When is the Sun actually on the Greenwich meridian?
why: It still needs 1°38.4′ to reach 360°: at 15° an hour that is 6m 34s, so 12 06 34 UT. That gap is the equation of time.

q: Two yachts in company talk on the SSB either side of 180°, each keeping its zone time. At 0003 UT on Thursday 12 November, what does each write in its log?
why: West of 180° (ZD −12): 0003 + 12 h = 1203 Thursday; east of it (ZD +12): 0003 − 12 h = 1203 Wednesday. Same clock, a day apart.

q: Running east at 48°S towards New Zealand at midsummer, you plan the evening stars. What window between civil and nautical twilight do you plan for?

q: You keep a rate book from the radio time signals. What daily rate do you write in it?
why: 7.2 s gained in 4½ days, from 3 Nov 0800 to 7 Nov 2000: 7.2 ÷ 4.5 = gaining 1.6 s a day.

q: Your morning sun sight works out to this LHA. How long until the Sun crosses your meridian for the noon sight?
why: The Sun is 360° − 341°15′ = 18°45′ east of your meridian; at 15° an hour, 18°45′ is 1h 15m.

a: About 0.02 s, far below sight accuracy
o: About 2 s, half a minute of longitude
About 0.5 s; subtract it from UT
About 4 s, a whole minute of longitude
why: 4000 M is about 7400 km; ÷ 300 000 km/s ≈ 0.025 s ≈ 0.006′ of longitude: ignore it.

q: Approaching Orkney from the Atlantic at midsummer, you want the time of sunrise for the morning sights. What is it in UT?

q: With 12 days to go to Barbados and no time signal, you know the watch's rate only to a second a day either way. How far off could your longitude be at landfall?
why: 12 days × 1 s = 12 s = 3′ of longitude; at 15°N, 3′ × cos 15° = 2.9 M east or west. The latitude is not affected.

fig.title: Landfall planning, no GPS
lines: Rate known to ±1 s a day

q: You leave Neiafu for Savusavu and tell friends in Fiji when to expect you. At what local time, and on which day, will you arrive?
why: UT out = 1900 Friday; + 2 d 5 h = 0000 UT Monday; Fiji is UT + 12: 1200 Monday. The date line bends east round Tonga.
ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

q: Before a sight you compare the deck watch with the chronometer below. What is the UT of the sight?
why: Chronometer now 5 + 4 × 1.5 = 11 s slow; the watch reads 13 s more, so it is 2 s fast: UT = 10 41 27 − 2 s = 10 41 25.
